01 / FLEX · TWO COMBUSTION REGIMES

Out of sight.
Still reacting.

A visible flame can disappear before combustion stops. Explore a simplified version of the two-stage droplet burning observed in FLEX.

How droplet combustion works

A liquid fuel droplet releases vapour, which mixes and reacts with oxygen in the surrounding air. The flame forms around the droplet, where these gases meet. In microgravity, the absence of buoyant rise allows a roughly spherical flame to form. The diagrams compare continued hot burning with the transition to cool burning observed under certain conditions in FLEX.

HOW A HOT FLAME STARTS

Energy starts the reaction.

Fuel vapour and oxygen need suitable conditions and an ignition source, such as a heated igniter. In a droplet experiment, the fuel vaporises and burns around the liquid. Once established, heat from combustion can sustain the reaction. This is the route shown in both panels.

HOW THIS COOL FLAME STARTS

The chemistry changes.

In the FLEX pathway, heat loss extinguishes the hot flame. Under certain fuel and atmosphere conditions, lower-temperature oxidation continues around the droplet. This does not happen after every fire goes out. Cool flames can also arise during heating or compression of suitable fuel–air mixtures; that is a different initiation route.

NASA: the FLEX discovery ↗
COOL DOES NOT MEAN SAFE

Less light. Different products.

Your notes use about 400 °C as a representative cool-flame temperature, not a universal threshold. Actual conditions vary. Low-temperature chemistry can produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde. Hot flames can also produce incomplete-combustion products: neither colour nor visibility establishes safe air.

NASA: cool-flame chemistry ↗
02 / ACME · FLAME DESIGN

Same fuel.
A different footprint.

Soot forms and grows in fuel-rich regions; some can oxidise before leaving the flame. Change these two processes separately to see why formation and emission are different.

How soot forms and leaves a flame

Soot consists of carbon-rich particles formed during incomplete combustion. Some of these particles are consumed by further chemical reactions before they leave the flame. This process is called oxidation. The diagrams distinguish soot formation from soot emission: the amount produced inside a flame is not necessarily the amount released into the exhaust.

Example dots in one animation cycle.
Not particle counts, mass, emissions or a NASA dataset.

01

1. Formation

In fuel-rich regions, where fuel is abundant relative to oxygen, incomplete combustion can produce carbon-rich particles. These particles may grow and join together. Peach dots represent soot forming within the flame.

→
02

2. Oxidation

Soot reacts with oxygen and other reactive species, consuming some of the solid particles. The blue dots fade to represent this removal. The amount consumed depends on the conditions and time available for reaction.

→
03

3. Emission

Particles that survive oxidation can leave the flame with the exhaust. Grey dots crossing the dashed line represent these emissions. Reducing formation and increasing oxidation are different ways to reduce the soot that escapes.

WHAT NASA STUDIED

Designing the flame, not just filtering the exhaust.

Your notes connect this to ACME’s Flame Design investigation, which studied soot control in spherical gaseous-fuel flames. The research aims to inform combustion systems with lower unwanted soot. Our demonstration explains the balance; it does not reproduce Flame Design data or establish which real-world operating conditions are best.

03 / KNOWLEDGE THAT TRAVELS

From the lab.
Into everyday life.

The research supports better models, better tests and better equipment. A promising application still needs engineering and validation on Earth.

FLEX → IGNITION CHEMISTRY → ENGINE DESIGN

How compression starts combustion

HCCI means Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition. A fuel–air mixture is compressed until it autoignites, rather than relying on a spark to start a travelling flame. Low-temperature chemistry influences when that happens.

Understanding that timing could support efficient, lower-emission combustion. HCCI is not an engine that stays at 400 °C, and a cool-flame observation alone does not establish fuel savings or an emissions reduction.

SoFIE / MATERIALS

Test the material.
Improve the screening.

Your notes describe tests of materials including plexiglass and cotton-based fabrics. Studying ignition and flame spread under controlled conditions can inform improved screening for materials used in buildings and transport. This is a research pathway, not a fire-safety rating for those materials.

NASA: SoFIE ↗
FIRES / PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT

Space materials.
Protection closer to home.

Project FIRES drew on Apollo-era materials and design ideas to improve firefighter equipment. A separate NASA technology-transfer route helped make breathing-air cylinders lighter. These are historical engineering applications, distinct from the combustion experiments above.

NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES ↗NASA: breathing apparatus ↗
